The reduced suspension of a pointed space $(X, x_0)$ is $\Sigma X = X \wedge S^1$, the smash product of $X$ with $S^1$. Thus
$$\Sigma S^{n-1} = S^{n-1} \wedge S^1.$$

The key ingredient is the following standard fact:

> **Lemma (Smash product of spheres).** For any $p, q \geq 0$, there is a canonical homeomorphism $S^p \wedge S^q \cong S^{p+q}$.

*Proof of Lemma.* Regard $S^p$ and $S^q$ as one-point compactifications of Euclidean spaces: $S^p = (\mathbb{R}^p)^+$ and $S^q = (\mathbb{R}^q)^+$, with basepoints at the respective points at infinity. For any locally compact Hausdorff spaces $X$ and $Y$, there is a canonical homeomorphism
$$X^+ \wedge Y^+ \;\cong\; (X \times Y)^+.$$

To see this, note that
$$X^+ \times Y^+ = (X \times Y) \;\sqcup\; \bigl(X \times \{\infty_Y\}\bigr) \;\sqcup\; \bigl(\{\infty_X\} \times Y\bigr) \;\sqcup\; \{(\infty_X, \infty_Y)\},$$
and the wedge $X^+ \vee Y^+ = X^+ \times \{\infty_Y\} \cup \{\infty_X\} \times Y^+$ is exactly the union of the last three pieces. Therefore the quotient $(X^+ \times Y^+)/(X^+ \vee Y^+)$ is $(X \times Y)$ together with a single point (the image of the collapsed wedge), which is precisely $(X \times Y)^+$. The map is the identity on $X \times Y$ and sends the entire wedge to the point at infinity. Since $X^+ \times Y^+$ is compact Hausdorff and $(X \times Y)^+$ is Hausdorff, this continuous bijection is a homeomorphism. $\square$

Applying the lemma with $X = \mathbb{R}^p$, $Y = \mathbb{R}^q$:
$$S^p \wedge S^q = (\mathbb{R}^p)^+ \wedge (\mathbb{R}^q)^+ \cong (\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^q)^+ = (\mathbb{R}^{p+q})^+ = S^{p+q}.$$

This homeomorphism is canonical: it uses only the canonical identification $\mathbb{R}^p \times \mathbb{R}^q = \mathbb{R}^{p+q}$ and the one-point compactification construction, which is functorial for locally compact Hausdorff spaces. No arbitrary choices are involved.

**Applying to our problem.** Set $p = n-1$ and $q = 1$:
$$\Sigma S^{n-1} = S^{n-1} \wedge S^1 \cong S^{(n-1)+1} = S^n.$$

It remains to connect this to the embedded sphere $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. The one-point compactification $(\mathbb{R}^n)^+$ is canonically homeomorphic to $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ via stereographic projection from the north pole $N = (0,\ldots,0,1)$: the inverse stereographic projection $\mathbb{R}^n \to S^n \setminus \{N\}$ extends to a homeomorphism $(\mathbb{R}^n)^+ \to S^n$ sending $\infty \mapsto N$. This is canonical given the standard embedding $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (the north pole is the distinguished point on the last coordinate axis).

Similarly, the basepoint $x_0 \in S^{n-1}$ (which is part of the data of the reduced suspension) determines the identification $S^{n-1} \cong (\mathbb{R}^{n-1})^+$ via stereographic projection from $x_0$, and the basepoint of $S^1$ determines $S^1 \cong (\mathbb{R})^+$.

- For a point represented by $(u, v) \in S^{n-1} \times S^1$ with $u \neq x_0$ and $v \neq s_0$: map to the point of $S^n \setminus \{N\} \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ corresponding to $(\sigma(u), \tau(v)) \in \mathbb{R}^{n-1} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^n$ under inverse stereographic projection.
- The collapsed wedge $S^{n-1} \vee S^1$ (a single point in $\Sigma S^{n-1}$) maps to the north pole $N \in S^n$.

This is a continuous bijection from the compact space $\Sigma S^{n-1}$ to the Hausdorff space $S^n$, hence a homeomorphism.

**Why it is canonical.** Each step in the composition
$$\Sigma S^{n-1} = S^{n-1} \wedge S^1 \;\cong\; (\mathbb{R}^{n-1} \times \mathbb{R})^+ \;=\; (\mathbb{R}^n)^+ \;\cong\; S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$$
is determined without arbitrary choices:
1. The smash product–to–one-point-compactification step $X^+ \wedge Y^+ \cong (X \times Y)^+$ is a canonical natural isomorphism.
2. The product identification $\mathbb{R}^{n-1} \times \mathbb{R} = \mathbb{R}^n$ is canonical.
3. The one-point compactification $(\mathbb{R}^n)^+ \cong S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ via stereographic projection is canonical given the standard embedding.

The only input data are the basepoint of $S^{n-1}$ (intrinsic to the definition of reduced suspension) and the standard embeddings $S^{n-1} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$, $S^n \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ (given in the problem). Given these, the homeomorphism is uniquely determined. $\blacksquare$
